lead: Time division multiplexing (TDM) lets many signals share one link by giving each a repeating slice of time, its slot. Each channel uses the whole bandwidth of the link, but only during its own slot. A frame marker tells the receiver where the round of slots starts, so it can hand each sample back to its channel. Digital telephone exchanges and trunks work this way: an E1 line at 2.048 Mbit/s carries 32 slots, 30 of them speech, and a T1 line carries 24 calls at 1.544 Mbit/s.
prereq: You need: PAM and PCM code words.

blocks.text: A commutator, a rotating switch in the classic picture and a multiplexer chip today, visits the N channels in turn and takes one sample from each per revolution. One revolution is a frame, and its duration is Tf = 1/fs, because each channel must be sampled at fs. For speech sampled at 8 kHz, Tf = 125 µs whatever the number of channels. Inside the frame each channel owns one time slot, and a synchronization bit or word marks the frame start. A guard time between slots absorbs timing error at the cost of some capacity.

All channels should be bandlimited by their own anti-aliasing filters before the commutator. If channels have different bandwidths, a wideband one can take several slots per frame (super-commutation) and a slow one a slot every few frames (sub-commutation). The receiver’s decommutator must turn in step with the transmitter’s, which is the whole difficulty of TDM.

sections.h3: PAM-TDM, PCM-TDM and the bit rate

blocks.text: In PAM-TDM each slot holds one analog sample. N channels sampled at fs give N fs pulses per second, and keeping them apart needs a minimum bandwidth of N fs/2; at the Nyquist rate that is N fm, the same total as FDM without guard bands. In PCM-TDM each slot holds an n-bit word, either kept together (word interleaving) or spread one bit per round (bit interleaving).

blocks.where: N data channels of n bits each, plus S framing and signalling bits per frame, at f<sub>s</sub> frames per second.

blocks.text: E1 uses slot 0 for frame alignment and alarms and slot 16 for signalling, leaving 30 speech slots. T1 takes signalling by robbing the least significant bit of each slot in every sixth frame. TDM, which multiplexes signals on one link, should not be confused with TDMA, a multiple-access method in which separate users take turns on a shared radio channel.

A single sync bit per frame is a weak marker, because data bits at the same position can imitate it for a while; T1 therefore spreads a fixed pattern over 12 or 24 frames, and E1 sends a 7-bit alignment word in slot 0 of alternate frames. The bit clock is recovered from transitions in the line signal, which the line code must supply.

If the receiver samples early it reads the tail of the previous slot; if late, the start of the next. Either way one channel leaks into its neighbour, which is TDM crosstalk; in PAM-TDM it also comes from a channel too narrow to let one pulse die out before the next. Losing frame alignment shifts every slot, so channel 1 is delivered as channel 2 until sync is found again. A frame slip is different: a whole frame is lost or repeated because the two clocks drift apart. TDM shares time, while frequency division multiplexing (see Frequency division multiplexing) shares frequency.

examples.question: Four signals bandlimited to 4 kHz are sampled at 8 kHz, coded with 8 bits and time multiplexed with one sync bit per frame. Find the frame duration, the bits per frame, R<sub>b</sub>, the bit duration and the slot duration.
steps: Bits per frame = N n + S = 4 × 8 + 1 = 33.
T<sub>b</sub> = 125 µs/33 = 3.79 µs; an 8-bit slot lasts 8 × 3.79 = 30.3 µs.
examples.answer: T<sub>f</sub> = 125 µs, 33 bits per frame, R<sub>b</sub> = 264 kbit/s, T<sub>b</sub> = 3.79 µs, slot 30.3 µs.

examples.question: Derive the line rates of T1 and E1 from their frames, and find the bit duration and the share of the line used by overhead in each.
steps: T1: 24 slots × 8 bits = 192 bits plus 1 framing bit = 193 bits per frame. R<sub>b</sub> = 193 × 8000 = 1 544 000 bit/s = 1.544 Mbit/s.
T1 bit duration = 1/1.544 × 10⁶ s = 0.648 µs; overhead = 1/193 = 0.52 % (8 kbit/s of framing).
E1: 32 slots × 8 bits = 256 bits per frame. R<sub>b</sub> = 256 × 8000 = 2 048 000 bit/s = 2.048 Mbit/s.
E1 bit duration = 1/2.048 × 10⁶ s = 0.488 µs; overhead = slots 0 and 16 = 2/32 = 6.25 % (128 kbit/s).
Both carry 64 kbit/s per speech channel: 24 × 64 = 1536 kbit/s and 30 × 64 = 1920 kbit/s of speech.
examples.answer: T1 1.544 Mbit/s (193-bit frames, 0.648 µs bits, 0.52 % overhead); E1 2.048 Mbit/s (256-bit frames, 0.488 µs bits, 6.25 % overhead).

traps: The frame rate is f<sub>s</sub> (8000 frames/s for speech), not R<sub>b</sub>, and it does not depend on N.
Count the overhead: use (N n + S) f<sub>s</sub>, not N n f<sub>s</sub>. E1’s 32 slots include two that carry no speech.
Slot duration and bit duration differ: in the 4-channel example a slot is 30.3 µs and a bit 3.79 µs.
TDM shares time and FDM shares frequency; TDMA is multiple access, not another name for TDM.

quiz.q: Define frame and slot in TDM.
quiz.a: A frame is one complete round of all channels, lasting 1/f<sub>s</sub>. A slot is the part of the frame given to one channel.

quiz.q: Why is a guard time used between slots?
quiz.a: It absorbs small timing errors and pulse spreading so that the receiver does not read part of the neighbouring slot; no data is sent in it, so it costs capacity.

quiz.q: Six channels are sampled at 8 kHz with 7 bits, plus 2 sync bits per frame. Find R<sub>b</sub>.
Find the minimum bandwidth of PAM-TDM for 24 channels bandlimited to 4 kHz and sampled at 8 kHz.
quiz.a: Pulse rate = 24 × 8000 = 192 000 pulses/s; B<sub>min</sub> = 192 000/2 = 96 kHz (= 24 × 4 kHz).

quiz.q: A TDM receiver clock runs slightly fast. Explain how crosstalk appears.
quiz.a: Each sampling instant comes a little earlier than the last, so the error grows. Once it exceeds the guard time, the receiver reads the tail of the previous slot and one channel leaks into another, until the sync pattern pulls the timing back.

quiz.q: Why do practical systems use a sync word or pattern rather than a single sync bit?
quiz.a: A single bit can be imitated by data at the same position, so the receiver may lock on a false position. A longer pattern, checked over several frames, is very unlikely to appear by chance, at the cost of a few extra bits.

beyond: Not for the exam. E1 and T1 are the bottom of the plesiochronous and SDH/SONET hierarchies, in which optical frames carry thousands of 64 kbit/s slots. Packet networks replaced fixed slots for data, but time-sensitive networking schedules Ethernet frames in slots again. Search next for SDH frame structure and time-sensitive networking.
